title: Anna's Courtroom Brilliance: The 'Chandrodayam' Trial
summary: Arguing his own case in court, Anna compared social plays to mirrors reflecting society's diseases: 'If a man dislikes his reflection, he should wash his face, not smash the mirror!'—winning complete dismissal of charges.
full_text:
In 1948, inside the crowded courthouse of Tiruchirappalli, a unique trial unfolded. Standing in the dock was C. N. Annadurai, the author of the revolutionary drama *Chandrodayam* (Moonrise). Standing beside him was a charismatic young stage actor named V. C. Ganesan—later to become India's legendary screen icon, Sivaji Ganesan!

The colonial-era police department had banned the play and prosecuted Anna for allegedly inciting civil unrest, subverting public morals, and ridiculing government authority.

Anna chose not to hire an advocate. "I shall defend the truth of my own art," he declared.

The public prosecutor delivered a fierce opening address:
"Your Honour, this drama mocks authority, exposes landlord exploitation, and incites class rebellion. It is toxic literature that damages public peace!"

The judge turned to Anna: "What is your defense, Mr. Annadurai?"

Anna rose serenely. Speaking in immaculate, courteous language, he asked:
"Your Honour! The prosecution calls my play 'toxic.' Let me ask:
If a physician examines a patient and diagnoses, 'You have a malignant tumor filled with pus,' did the physician create the tumor, or did he merely diagnose the disease?

My drama is simply a mirror held up to the face of society! It reflects the caste prejudice, feudal cruelty, and poverty that crush our people.
If a man looks into a mirror and dislikes the dirt on his face, he should wash his face—he should not smash the mirror!
My play is that mirror. Smashed mirrors do not cure diseased faces!"

The court was spellbound.

The prosecutor interjected: "The final act depicts a revolt of the oppressed. Is that not inciting violence?"

Anna smiled gently:
"Revolt does not come from a stage dialogue; it is born in the hungry bellies of the oppressed!
If demanding bread for the hungry is revolt, then I plead guilty!
If exposing injustice is subversion, then I am a subversives!
But courts exist not as fortresses of oppression, but as sanctuaries of justice. I stand before this court confident that truth will prevail."

The judge dismissed all charges, lifting the ban on the play. Sivaji Ganesan touched Anna's feet in tears of relief and reverence.
moral: Art and literature are society's mirrors; suppressing truth never cures the underlying injustice.
witty_quote: Plays do not create social sickness; they are mirrors reflecting the truth!
